# `silk/bench/bencher`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Benchmarks declared with `bench fn`, the [`Bencher`](#Bencher) they loop on, and the program that
runs them.

## When to use
Write a `bench fn` beside the code it measures when the work is a Silk function: a parser,
a hash, one step of a computation. Compare whole programs, or programs in other languages,
with a suite of `silk.bench.suite` instead.

## Details
A benchmark is a top-level function marked `bench` that takes one [`Bencher`](#Bencher). It does its
setup, then loops on [`Bencher.next`](#Bencher.impl.next), and each turn of the loop is one iteration:

```silk,ignore
bench fn sumToOneThousand(b: Bencher) {
  let mut total: u64 = 0
  while b.next() {
    total = 0
    let mut at: u64 = 0
    while at < 1000 {
      total = total + at
      at = at + 1
    }
    b.keep<u64>(&total)
  }
  b.check(total)
}
```

The time that counts runs from the first call of `next` to the call that returns `false`,
so what comes before the loop and after it is free. [`Bencher.stop`](#Bencher.impl.stop) and [`Bencher.start`](#Bencher.impl.start)
leave a stretch inside the loop out, and [`Bencher.reset`](#Bencher.impl.reset) starts the time again.

The benchmarks of a program are the `bench` functions of the modules its entry file
imports, directly or through other modules of the same package. [`Benchmarks.main`](#Benchmarks.impl.main) runs
them. A program whose `main` calls it is a harness as `silk.bench.harness` describes: run
by hand, it finds an iteration count for each benchmark, takes ten samples and prints
result lines; declared in a suite with `silk.bench.suite.Implementation.driven`, it takes
its iteration counts from the benchmark task, which compares it with other programs and
with earlier runs.

A benchmark is named after its function. Two benchmarks with one name in different modules
are both named `<module>.<name>`.

A `bench effect fn` may fail. A failure ends the run of that benchmark, which is reported as
failed.

## Gotchas
- The compiler removes work whose result nothing uses. Give each iteration's result to
  [`Bencher.keep`](#Bencher.impl.keep).
- The compiler also computes ahead of time what it can: work on a constant is done when the
  program is built. Give [`Bencher.keep`](#Bencher.impl.keep) the input too, before the work reads it.
- `bench` marks only a top-level function with one parameter, no type parameters and no
  requirement row. A benchmark that needs a service provides it inside.
- A benchmark that never calls `next` is timed as a whole, as if its one call were every
  iteration.
- A build that does not call [`Benchmarks.main`](#Benchmarks.impl.main) keeps no benchmark.

## Examples
The entry file of a benchmark program:

```silk,ignore
import silk.bench.bencher { Benchmarks }
import silk.system.host_input { HostInput }

// The modules that hold the `bench` functions. A name that starts with `_` is not
// reported as unused.
import parser as _parser
import encoder as _encoder

pub effect fn main() -> i32
  ? &mut HostInput {
  return run Benchmarks.main()
}
```

Import as `Bencher` with `import silk.bench.bencher { Bencher }`.

## `Bencher`

```silk
pub struct Bencher
```

The run of a benchmark that is in progress: what a `bench fn` loops on.

### Details
A `Bencher` is a handle to a run the benchmark program holds, so a copy of it is the same
run.

### Gotchas
A `Bencher` is good only inside the call of the benchmark it was given to.

<a id="Bencher.impl.next"></a>

### Method `next`

```silk
pub fn next(self: Self) -> bool
```

Returns whether there is another iteration to do. The first call starts the time, and the
call that returns `false` stops it.

<a id="Bencher.impl.iterations"></a>

### Method `iterations`

```silk
pub fn iterations(self: Self) -> u64
```

Returns how many iterations the run has in all.

<a id="Bencher.impl.stop"></a>

### Method `stop`

```silk
pub fn stop(self: Self) -> ()
```

Stops the time, until [`Bencher.start`](#Bencher.impl.start). Stopping twice changes nothing.

<a id="Bencher.impl.start"></a>

### Method `start`

```silk
pub fn start(self: Self) -> ()
```

Starts the time again after [`Bencher.stop`](#Bencher.impl.stop). Starting twice changes nothing.

<a id="Bencher.impl.reset"></a>

### Method `reset`

```silk
pub fn reset(self: Self) -> ()
```

Starts the time again from zero, after work inside the loop that should not count.

<a id="Bencher.impl.keep"></a>

### Method `keep`

```silk
pub fn keep<T>(self: Self, value: &T) -> ()
```

Makes the compiler treat `value` as used, so it cannot remove the work that computed it.

#### Gotchas
On a target without inline assembly, which is every target but Linux on x86_64 and
aarch64 and macOS on aarch64, the value is only made to live in memory, which stops less.

<a id="Bencher.impl.check"></a>

### Method `check`

```silk
pub fn check(self: Self, number: u64) -> ()
```

Reports `number` as what the run computed, such as a checksum. A benchmark task does not
compare implementations whose checks differ.

<a id="Benchmarks.impl.names"></a>

### Associated function `names`

```silk
pub effect fn names() -> List<String>
    ! OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Allocator
```

Returns the names of the benchmarks of the program, in the order they run: by module,
then by name.

#### Errors
`OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply the names.

<a id="Benchmarks.impl.perform"></a>

### Associated function `perform`

```silk
pub effect fn perform() -> ()
    ! TransportError | OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Transport | &mut Allocator | &mut MonotonicClock | &mut HostInput
```

Runs the benchmarks as a harness: driven by a benchmark task when one started the
program, and otherwise alone, printing result lines.

#### Errors
- `TransportError` if a line cannot be carried.
- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply a line.

<a id="Benchmarks.impl.serve"></a>

### Associated function `serve`

```silk
pub effect fn serve(driven: bool) -> ()
    ! TransportError | OutOfMemoryError
    ? &mut Transport | &mut Allocator | &mut MonotonicClock
```

Runs the benchmarks as a harness that follows the commands arriving over the `Transport`
if `driven`, and that otherwise runs every benchmark itself and sends the result lines.

#### Errors
- `TransportError` if a line cannot be carried.
- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply a line.

<a id="Benchmarks.impl.main"></a>

### Associated function `main`

```silk
pub effect fn main() -> i32
    ? &mut HostInput
```

Runs the benchmarks with the standard input and output of the process, and returns the
exit status: 0, or 1 if a line could not be carried.
